strengths: Soundness: The paper evaluates six personas on two widely used open-weight models, considers both amplification and suppression, and compares five intervention sites using trait–coherency Pareto frontiers. The held-out queries, five-run averaging, ablations, and MMLU/PPL/IFEval measurements provide multiple forms of evidence for the basic empirical result that targeted head intervention can outperform residual-stream steering.

Originality: Localizing a small set of candidate “Style Modulation Heads” through layer-wise vector geometry and head contribution scores is an interesting treatment of the underexplored question of where to steer. The combination of geometric localization with head-level intervention is more informative than another residual-stream steering variant.

Significance: If validated more rigorously, steering only a few heads could offer a useful, computationally lightweight way to control high-level behavior while preserving generation quality. The asymmetric collapse under out-of-distribution steering is also a practically relevant observation.

Presentation: The main narrative is generally clear, and the layer-to-head localization progression is easy to follow. The paper supplies system prompts, judge prompts, qualitative generations, complete Pareto plots, and an honest limitations section noting restricted persona and architecture coverage.
The authors attempt human validation of the LLM judge using three annotators and report roughly 92% pairwise agreement, which is preferable to relying entirely on an unvalidated automatic metric.
weaknesses: Soundness: The evidence does not support the strong claim that three heads “independently govern” persona or are functionally specialized style modules. Heads are selected by alignment with the aggregate persona direction and then tested on closely related data generated using the same system-prompt templates. The ablation is sequential, lacks matched random-head or same-layer controls, and can establish causal contribution but not exclusivity, independence, or specialization.

The paper infers that style heads are orthogonal to factual knowledge and instruction-following circuits because ablation preserves MMLU and IFEval. This conflicts with the paper’s own Section 3 result that these benchmarks can remain stable despite substantial generation degradation. Stability on two coarse benchmarks is insufficient evidence for circuit orthogonality.

The primary metrics are vulnerable to circularity and judge bias. Human pairs were preselected using extreme GPT-4.1-mini scores, so high forced-choice agreement does not validate score calibration, the threshold of 80, or small differences between Pareto frontiers. The coherency rubric is internally inconsistent: it defines 100 as containing no hallucinations but then says a completely incorrect answer may score 100. No alternative judges, blinded absolute ratings, inter-human agreement, or uncertainty analysis are reported.

Results are averaged over five runs, but the plots and tables provide no variances, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This matters because several claimed Pareto advantages are small. The coefficient ranges are also extended until a peak is observed, creating a potentially post-hoc and unequal search budget across intervention types.

There is a serious reporting inconsistency: every Qwen2.5-7B entry in Appendix Table 13 is exactly duplicated in the Llama-3.1-8B columns, despite the models having visibly different frontiers elsewhere. Figure 11 is in the Llama appendix but its caption identifies Qwen layer 20 and Qwen heads. These apparent copy errors undermine confidence in the quantitative appendix.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The title page contains an empty “Code:” field, and the manuscript does not provide code, the extraction/evaluation query sets, random seeds, token limits, precise activation-hook implementation, hardware, or enough API/version detail to reconstruct the logit-based GPT judge. System prompts and coefficient grids are useful but insufficient for reproducing the central results.

The comparison is limited to intervention locations under the authors’ basic addition method. Although angular and dynamic steering methods are discussed as approaches designed to reduce degradation, they are not included experimentally. Thus the evidence establishes an advantage over coarse activation addition, not broadly superior robust steering.

Generalization is narrow: only two dense 7B–8B instruction models receive full evaluation, while the claimed MoE extension is mentioned only briefly without results. Evaluation queries change, but persona prompt templates do not, leaving open whether the shared heads capture generic system-instruction/style contrasts rather than persona formation broadly.

Ethics and limitations treatment is incomplete. The method explicitly strengthens malicious and hallucinating behavior, yet there is no dedicated misuse analysis, release plan, or safeguards discussion. The human study also omits consent, compensation, recruitment, and review details. The stated architecture/persona limitations are candid, but they do not address these evaluation and ethical issues.

Presentation contains overclaims such as “noise-free steering,” “dedicated” heads, and practical safety benefits without direct measurement of off-target noise or realistic safety outcomes. The arbitrary coherency threshold and newly introduced envelope score receive no sensitivity analysis.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper asks a useful and relatively underexplored “where to steer” question. Decomposing attention outputs and targeting a few heads is a simple, potentially practical alternative to residual-stream intervention.

Soundness: The empirical scope is reasonably broad, covering two open 7–8B instruction-tuned models, six personas, both amplification and suppression, five intervention sites, and several utility metrics. Evaluating trait–coherency Pareto frontiers is more informative than comparing methods at one arbitrary coefficient.

Presentation: The main motivation and experimental narrative are generally easy to follow, and the appendix includes prompts, coefficient ranges, comprehensive frontier plots, and qualitative generations that illustrate collapse.
The authors attempt human validation of the LLM judge and honestly acknowledge limited architectural and persona generalization. These limitations themselves should not be penalized.
weaknesses: Soundness—central mechanistic claim: The evidence does not support the assertion that three heads “independently govern” persona or constitute specialized Style Modulation Heads. The contribution score selects heads whose difference-in-means outputs align with the aggregate difference vector, so finding contributors to that same vector is partly built into the definition. Steering and zero ablation establish influence, not specialization or exclusive causal mediation.

Soundness—missing controls: The ablations are cumulative and lack same-layer random, output-norm-matched, and contribution-matched head controls. There is also no cross-persona transfer matrix, alternative contrast construction, or held-out persona experiment to rule out that the common heads encode generic system-prompt compliance, affect, or departure from the shared “helpful assistant” baseline rather than persona/style specifically.

Soundness—evaluation validity: Nearly all central conclusions depend on GPT-4.1-mini scores. The coherency rubric is internally inconsistent: a score of 100 is defined as containing no hallucinations, but the judge is then told not to assess correctness and that a completely incorrect answer may score 100. This particularly complicates the hallucination persona and weakens claims about semantic collapse and safety.

The human validation does not repair this issue. It uses only 10 pairs per persona and deliberately selects easy extremes (e.g., scores above 80 versus 10–30) using the same LLM scores being validated. It therefore does not validate continuous scores, the consequential coherency threshold of 80, or close comparisons between Pareto frontiers. Inter-annotator agreement and uncertainty are not reported.

Soundness/statistics: Despite stating that experiments use five runs, plots and tables provide no confidence intervals, variance, hypothesis tests, or uncertainty for Pareto areas. Head selection, layer selection, coefficient sweeps, and evaluation occur on closely related prompt constructions; coefficients are even extended post hoc “until the peak score was observed.” No separate selection/tuning split is described, making the reported win counts vulnerable to selection bias.

Presentation/reliability: The appendix contains serious inconsistencies. Table 13 reports exactly identical Qwen and Llama values throughout, strongly suggesting a copy or computation error. Figure 11 is in the Llama section but its caption describes Qwen layer 20 and Qwen heads; Figure 15 repeats “Hallucination” where one row appears to be Humorous; and several figure references/captions are incorrect. These errors reduce confidence in the result pipeline.

Reproducibility is inadequate: The manuscript contains an empty “Code:” field, provides no implementation, and does not include the extraction/evaluation query sets, complete generation settings, exact judge snapshot/API configuration, seeds, or sufficient details for reproducing intervention hooks and Pareto computation. The unreported Qwen3-MoE experiment is nevertheless asserted in the limitations.

Significance/generalization: Results are confined to two similarly sized dense instruction models and six heavily prompted traits. The manuscript makes broader claims about functional modularity, safer deployment, and preservation of reasoning without larger-scale models, standard safety evaluations, adversarial testing, or comparisons with stronger steering approaches beyond intervention-location variants.

Ethics: The work deliberately elicits malicious and fabricated outputs but offers no concrete misuse analysis, release safeguards, or discussion of annotator consent, compensation, and exposure to harmful material. The impact statement presents only benefits. These concerns are addressable, but the current treatment is incomplete.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper asks a useful and comparatively underexplored question—where to apply activation steering—and proposes a simple, computationally attractive localization method based on layer-wise geometry and head-contribution scores. Targeting a few heads could be practically valuable for controllable generation.

Soundness: The empirical story is coherent across two model families, six personas, and both trait amplification and suppression. The strongest result is the Pareto comparison: head-localized steering is best in 11/12 Qwen2.5-7B conditions and 9/12 Llama-3.1-8B conditions in Table 1, with especially consistent gains for trait suppression.

Soundness: The paper uses several complementary analyses—representation geometry, head-wise interventions, zero ablation, coherency/trait Pareto frontiers, and MMLU, perplexity, and IFEval—rather than relying on a single probe or benchmark.

Evaluation: Averaging generation experiments over five runs is helpful, and the authors attempt to validate GPT-4.1-mini judgments with three human annotators. The reported pairwise human–LLM agreement exceeds 90% overall for both trait and coherency comparisons.

Presentation: The main argument is easy to follow, figures communicate the principal trends effectively, and the appendix provides prompts, coefficient ranges, qualitative examples, and expanded results.

Limitations: The manuscript candidly identifies restricted architectural and persona coverage, including a differing multi-transition pattern in Gemma3. This honest discussion appropriately tempers the generality of the findings.
weaknesses: Soundness: The evidence supports that selected heads are effective intervention sites, but not the stronger claims that they independently govern persona formation, are functionally specialized, or improve steering specifically by avoiding “off-target noise.” Noise is never directly defined or measured, and alternative explanations—such as differences in vector direction, scale, or model sensitivity at the selected site—are not ruled out.

Soundness: The ablation study is not a sufficiently controlled causal test of specialization. Heads are cumulatively removed across layers, the comparison layers are chosen because they already exhibited weaker steering effects, and there are no random-head, magnitude-matched, or equally important general-purpose-head controls. Individual and non-cumulative ablations would be substantially more diagnostic.

Evaluation: The main outcomes depend heavily on one proprietary LLM judge. Human validation uses only extreme pairs selected using the LLM’s own scores, such as scores above 80 versus 10–30. This circular, easy-separation design does not validate absolute scores, mid-range rankings, small differences between Pareto curves, or the consequential coherency threshold of 80. Inter-annotator agreement is also not reported.

Evaluation: The coherency rubric is internally ambiguous: it says a score of 100 contains no hallucinations, but subsequently instructs the judge not to assess correctness and allows a completely incorrect answer to score 100. For the hallucination persona in particular, a judge without references may detect stylistic confidence rather than factual fabrication.

Statistical support: Despite temperature-1 generation and five runs, the paper reports no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Consequently, it is difficult to know whether some relatively close Pareto differences are robust. Head discovery and evaluation also appear to reuse the same persona definitions without a separate localization-validation split.

Baseline calibration: Intervention sites use different extracted vectors and coefficient ranges, with ranges extended adaptively until a peak is observed. Pareto analysis reduces sensitivity to raw coefficient scale, but the protocol still gives limited assurance that every baseline received an equally thorough and prospectively specified search. Sensitivity to the chosen envelope definition and τ=80 is not shown.

Generality: Results are primarily demonstrated on two similarly sized, instruction-tuned, open-weight models and six strongly prompt-defined traits. The stated MoE extension is not accompanied by quantitative results, while the preliminary Gemma3 result already departs from the proposed single-transition localization picture.

Reproducibility/presentation: The manuscript’s “Code:” field is blank, and important details such as exact extraction/evaluation queries, random seeds, generation-length settings, and complete implementation instructions are not supplied. There are also visible consistency errors: Table 13 repeats identical Qwen and Llama values, and Figure 11’s caption describes Qwen heads although the section and plot concern Llama.

Ethics: Steering toward malicious and hallucinating behavior has clear dual-use implications, yet the impact statement discusses only benefits. The paper should address release safeguards and report consent, compensation, and risk mitigation for annotators exposed to potentially harmful generations.

strengths: Originality and significance: The paper asks a useful, underexplored “where to steer” question and proposes a simple component-level alternative to residual-stream activation steering. Localizing persona control to a few attention heads could materially improve controllability and mechanistic understanding.

Empirical breadth: The main experiments cover six diverse personas, two instruction-tuned model families, positive and negative steering, five intervention sites, and several utility metrics. The reported Pareto frontiers generally favor correlated-head steering, especially for trait suppression.

Causal evidence: Head-level steering is complemented by sequential zero ablations and random/lower-impact controls. The observed reduction in persona expression without corresponding drops in MMLU, IFEval, or judged coherency is suggestive of functional specialization rather than correlation alone.

Presentation and limitations: The main narrative is coherent, the geometric localization procedure is reasonably clear, and the appendices provide prompts, coefficient ranges, qualitative samples, additional plots, and preliminary analyses of Gemma-3-12B and Qwen3-30B-A3B. The authors appropriately acknowledge that localization changes across architectures and that the work addresses only the intervention-location axis.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim that three heads “independently govern” persona/style is stronger than the evidence. Steering establishes sufficiency and sequential ablation suggests relevance, but neither establishes exclusivity or mediation. Ablating the selected heads leaves substantial trait expression, the ablation accumulates heads across several layers, and comparable causal controls are limited.

The principal outcome is a GPT-4.1-mini score, yet its validation is weak and partly circular: examples are first selected using that judge’s extreme score ranges and humans then compare only 10 deliberately high-versus-low pairs per persona. This tests easy rank ordering rather than calibration, reliability near the coherency threshold, or robustness on unselected samples. It is especially concerning because judged coherency determines the claimed Pareto advantage.

Statistical support is inadequate. Although results are said to average five runs, the main curves and Pareto tables provide no confidence intervals, run-level variability, or significance tests. Head/layer selection, coefficient-range extension, and comparison appear to reuse the same evaluation setting, leaving unquantified selection bias.

The Pareto analysis is insufficiently specified for the suppression condition. Equation (5) always maximizes the trait score, whereas Target-minus-alpha is described as preferring lower trait scores; the apparent transformation producing near-100 suppression scores is not defined. The custom threshold tau=80 and envelope-area summary also receive no sensitivity analysis.

Generalization is overstated. The full Pareto comparison is demonstrated only on Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B. The additional Gemma and Qwen3 studies are preliminary, apparently use a narrower analysis, and actually show that the proposed single-transition localization heuristic does not cleanly transfer. No held-out personas test whether the same heads generalize beyond the traits used to identify them.

Reproducibility is presently poor: the title page contains a blank “Code:” field, the extraction and held-out evaluation queries are not supplied, and implementation details such as exact intervention equations for selected heads, random-head sampling, seeds, generation limits, model revisions, and API settings are missing. Reliance on a proprietary judge further complicates exact reproduction.

Presentation and ethics: Several broad mechanistic and safety claims—such as off-target noise being the cause of collapse, preserved “general reasoning,” and safer deployment—are not directly established by the experiments. The impact statement discusses benefits but not the obvious dual-use risk of efficiently inducing malicious, deceptive, sycophantic, or hallucinating behavior, nor safeguards for releasing such steering tools.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper asks a useful, comparatively underexplored question—where activation steering should be applied—and proposes a simple geometric procedure for identifying persona-associated attention heads.

Soundness: Experiments span six personas and two principal model families, include both amplification and suppression, and compare residual-stream, attention-output, and head-level interventions. The Pareto plots provide some evidence that targeted interventions can improve the empirical trait–coherency tradeoff.

The head-level results are supported by several complementary analyses: contribution scores, individual-head steering, sequential ablation, random-head controls, and comparisons using cosine similarity rather than an unnormalized dot product.

The appendix is unusually extensive, providing system prompts, judge prompts, coefficient ranges, qualitative outputs, general-capability results, and preliminary analyses of Gemma-3-12B and Qwen3-30B-A3B.

Presentation is generally well organized, and the paper honestly acknowledges that localization differs in larger or architecturally distinct models and that it does not investigate how- or when-to-steer methods.
weaknesses: Soundness: The paper does not establish its central mechanistic explanation that residual-stream intervention amplifies “off-target noise.” No off-target component or noise is defined or measured, and no experiment decomposes the alleged noise or shows that removing it mediates the coherency improvement. The results support an intervention-location effect, not the claimed causal mechanism.

The “independently govern,” “trait-dedicated,” and “functionally specialized” claims are substantially stronger than the evidence. The same heads responding to six highly stylized target-versus-neutral prompt contrasts could reflect shared system-prompt, affect, or response-style features. Ablation establishes necessity under these prompts but not independence or specificity; only a narrow set of general benchmarks is used as a negative control.

The main quantitative Pareto metric appears inconsistent with the suppression objective. Equation 5 defines an upper envelope that maximizes trait score, but Target−α is described as optimal toward the upper-left, where trait expression is minimized. The manuscript does not define a transformation such as 100−trait for this condition, yet Table 1 reports larger values as better. This makes a central cross-method summary difficult to interpret or verify.

The primary coherency judge explicitly instructs GPT-4.1-mini not to assess correctness or logical validity and says a completely incorrect answer may receive 100. This conflicts with the paper's earlier definition of coherency as including absence of hallucinations and weakens claims about generation quality and safety. It may chiefly measure surface readability, such as capitalization and repetition.

The human validation does not validate the absolute 0–100 scores or the crucial threshold τ=80. Pairs were selected using extreme LLM-judge scores and humans merely chose which member ranked higher, creating an easy, selection-conditioned agreement test. There is no random-sample evaluation, calibration analysis, inter-annotator agreement, uncertainty estimate, or validation near the decision threshold.

Statistical support is inadequate despite five generation runs: plots and tables provide no confidence intervals, variance, hypothesis tests, or uncertainty for Pareto rankings. Coefficient ranges are unequal across methods and are adaptively extended “until the peak score was observed,” which introduces additional selection flexibility without a prespecified stopping rule.

Generalization is limited. The complete tradeoff evaluation is confined to two similarly sized instruct models. Results on Gemma and Qwen3 are described as preliminary, reveal that the proposed single-transition localization pattern fails, and do not reproduce the full intervention comparison. Thus the broad claim of a general localization framework is premature.

Reproducibility is insufficient for acceptance. The manuscript's “Code:” field is blank; the exact evaluation queries, generated outputs, seeds, implementation hooks, benchmark configurations, and complete judge-call settings are not supplied. Reliance on a proprietary GPT-4.1-mini judge further limits exact reproduction. Presentation contains several overstatements and inconsistencies—for example, a figure-reference typo for IFEval, terminology changes such as Neutral+α versus Neg+Add, and conclusions about safer deployment that are not supported by an actual safety evaluation.

Ethics and limitations treatment is incomplete. The work deliberately strengthens malicious and hallucinating behavior, but the impact statement discusses only benefits and offers no misuse analysis or release safeguards. The human-study description reports that annotators were non-native English speakers but omits consent, compensation, recruitment, and ethics-review information. The limitations section discusses architecture and steering granularity but not these evaluation, causal-identification, or dual-use limitations.

strengths: Soundness: The central empirical result is supported by complementary evidence: layer-wise geometric analysis, individual-head interventions, cumulative zero ablations, random-head controls, and trait–coherency Pareto comparisons. The strongest evaluation covers six traits and two model families over five runs.

Significance: Identifying where to intervene is a useful and practical complement to work on how and when to steer. Targeting only a few heads frequently preserves coherence substantially better than residual-stream steering, especially when suppressing an induced trait.

Originality: The combination of geometric localization with head-specific persona steering is a novel and conceptually appealing contribution. The observation that the same small set of heads affects multiple stylistic/persona traits is particularly interesting.

Presentation: The paper is well organized, motivates the coherence problem clearly, and provides extensive appendices with prompts, coefficient ranges, qualitative generations, full Pareto plots, ablations, and additional architectures.
The evaluation does not rely exclusively on coherence: it also reports MMLU, IFEval, and perplexity, and candidly notes cases where head steering is not best on general-capability metrics.

The limitations discussion appropriately acknowledges that localization changes across architectures and that the study addresses only the intervention-location dimension. Preliminary Gemma-3 and Qwen3-MoE results broaden the empirical picture rather than hiding this limitation.
weaknesses: The mechanistic interpretation is stronger than the evidence warrants. The experiments show that selected heads are effective intervention sites, but do not directly establish that residual steering fails because it amplifies “off-target noise,” nor that the heads independently “govern” persona formation. Alternative explanations such as favorable scaling, routing, or representational alignment are not ruled out.

Head discovery and headline evaluation use the same six personas. Held-out questions reduce prompt-instance overfitting, but there is no held-out-trait test showing that the geometric selection rule discovers useful heads for an unseen persona. This weakens the claimed general localization framework.

The primary trait and coherence results depend heavily on GPT-4.1-mini. Human validation uses only ten deliberately easy, widely separated pairs per persona (e.g., scores above 80 versus 10–30), selected using the judge scores themselves. It therefore does not validate numerical calibration or comparisons near the coherence threshold of 80 that determine the Pareto metric. Inter-annotator agreement is also not reported.

Although results are averaged over five stochastic runs, plots and tables provide no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance analysis. Consequently, close Pareto-score differences and claims of consistent superiority cannot be assessed statistically. The newly introduced envelope-area score is also sensitive to the fixed, insufficiently justified coherence threshold and sampled coefficient grid.

Generalization is uneven. The clean single-layer localization found in Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B does not hold for Gemma-3-12B or Qwen3-30B-A3B; those appendix experiments are preliminary and omit the full Pareto comparison and ablation evidence used to support the main claim.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript shows a blank code field, does not provide all extraction/evaluation queries or generated outputs, and leaves some implementation details of head-level intervention and judge aggregation underspecified. The ethics discussion emphasizes benefits but does not adequately discuss dual-use risks from amplifying malicious, deceptive, or hallucinating behavior.
